# The Great Indian Dream Liner

### How India’s Software Revolution Empowered a Generation of Women, Enriched Families, and Quietly Stole Everyone’s Evenings

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

There was a time in middle-class India when matrimonial negotiations resembled the selection process for a cultural academy.

The girl could sing a kriti in Kalyani.

She could identify the difference between Bhairavi and Kambhoji before most people had finished their second coffee.

She knew embroidery, rangoli, devotional songs, and possessed a collection of stainless-steel vessels substantial enough to survive a minor war.

Parents announced with great pride:

*“Our daughter has completed B.Sc. Mathematics and has learned Carnatic music for ten years.”*

The neighbours nodded approvingly.

The aunties took notes.

The groom’s family looked impressed.

Then the 1990s arrived.

The economy opened.

Satellite television appeared.

Computers invaded India.

And three new deities entered the middle-class pantheon: Infosys, TCS and Wipro.

Almost overnight, centuries of cultural qualifications were condensed into one glorious sentence:

**“Our daughter works in IT.”**

That single line achieved what ten years of music lessons, Sanskrit slokas, and university medals could not.

It raised family status.

It impressed relatives.

It silenced critics.

It caused neighbouring mothers to immediately enquire about engineering college admissions.

By the late 1990s, “Our daughter is going onsite” had replaced “Our daughter is performing at Navaratri golu” as the ultimate parental boast.

And honestly, who could blame them?

For the first time in Indian history, millions of women entered a profession that offered something their mothers and grandmothers rarely possessed:

Financial independence.

Not symbolic independence.

Not theoretical independence.

Actual money arriving every month into an account bearing their own name.

It was revolutionary.

And it was wonderful.

The story deserves celebration.

But every revolution leaves behind a few unintended consequences.

The Green Revolution gave us food security and diabetes.

Television gave us entertainment and political shouting matches.

The IT Revolution gave us prosperity and Outlook Calendar.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Visa God and the Great Indian Migration

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If you were around in the late 1990s, you will remember the atmosphere.

India was drunk on possibility.

Y2K had arrived like an unexpected wedding guest carrying gifts.

American companies were terrified their computers would collapse at midnight.

Indian software engineers became the emergency plumbers of the digital world.

Money flowed.

Projects multiplied.

Hope became a national industry.

Entire families began worshipping a new deity.

Not Vishnu.

Not Shiva.

Not Lakshmi.

The Visa God.

Special prayers were conducted for H-1B approvals.

Astrologers discovered expertise in immigration law.

Temple visits increased dramatically whenever the US Consulate announced interview dates.

A daughter travelling to Dallas generated more excitement than a cousin’s engagement.

When she returned home six months later carrying chocolates from Costco and stories about highways wider than Tamil Nadu, she became a local celebrity.

The first generation genuinely believed technology would create a perfect life.

A global career.

Financial stability.

Modern living.

Freedom.

Balance.

And for a brief moment, it looked as though they were right.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# When Engineers Became Resources

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The trouble began when success scaled.

Every industry behaves beautifully when it is small.

A small restaurant serves wonderful food.

A small school knows every student.

A small company remembers every employee’s birthday.

Then growth arrives.

And spreadsheets replace relationships.

The software industry discovered this truth with remarkable efficiency.

By the 2010s, software engineering increasingly resembled manufacturing.

People became resources.

Managers became dashboards.

Human beings became utilisation metrics.

Someone somewhere decided that every aspect of life required a framework.

Agile arrived.

Then Scrum.

Then SaaS.

Then enough frameworks to require additional frameworks explaining the previous frameworks.

Meetings multiplied like rabbits.

Stand-ups became sit-downs.

Sit-downs became workshops.

Workshops became alignment sessions.

Alignment sessions required pre-alignment sessions.

Soon a software engineer’s primary responsibility was no longer writing software.

It was attending meetings about writing software.

An average professional woman now spends half her day discussing work and the other half completing the work she discussed.

Often after dinner.

Sometimes after midnight.

Occasionally after questioning every life choice that brought her here.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Socialist Luxury We Never Valued

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Perhaps this is where nostalgia enters the story.

Not nostalgia for shortages.

Not nostalgia for Ambassador cars.

Certainly not nostalgia for waiting seven years for a telephone connection.

But nostalgia for something that quietly disappeared.

Time.

Community.

Neighbourhood.

Human scale.

I grew up in Neyveli.

Those who grew up there know what I mean.

Neyveli was one of independent India’s great socialist experiments.

A town built not merely to extract lignite but to produce citizens.

There were libraries.

Parks.

Tree-lined avenues.

Sports grounds.

Schools.

Community centres.

Book clubs.

Debates.

Music classes.

The famous Central Library where children spent long summer afternoons escaping both the heat and reality.

Under rain trees, engineers discussed politics.

Teachers debated literature.

Doctors argued economics.

Nobody called it networking.

Nobody called it community engagement.

People simply existed together.

The township assumed something radical:

Human beings were more than economic units.

Replace Neyveli with any other Town, same story would repeat.

Today a young IT professional may earn ten times what her mother earned.

Yet she often has less leisure than her grandmother.

Her grandmother had fewer appliances but more conversations.

Her mother had less money but more evenings.

She has food-delivery apps, cloud storage, high-speed internet and premium streaming subscriptions.

She also has seventeen unread emails at midnight.

Progress is a funny thing.

It solves old problems and invents new ones.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Gastro-Corporate Republic

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every civilization leaves behind a culinary legacy.

The Cholas gave us temple cuisine.

The Mughals gave us biryani.

The IT industry appears determined to be remembered for cold pasta eaten during conference calls.

Observe the dietary habits of the modern software professional.

Breakfast consists of coffee.

Lunch arrives via an app.

Dinner occurs whenever the client in New Jersey permits it.

Swiggy and Zomato now know more about dietary habits than most grandparents.

The refrigerator contains almond milk, three sauces nobody remembers buying, expired vegetables and profound guilt.

Corporate cafeterias deserve their own chapter in Indian history.

They possess the remarkable ability to produce food simultaneously labelled Italian, Chinese and Healthy while offending Italy, China and nutrition science.

Midnight Maggi has become both a comfort food and an incident management protocol.

Meanwhile the human body quietly files complaints.

Vitamin D deficiency has become a national software standard.

Many professionals move daily between apartment, cab, office and laptop without meaningful interaction with sunlight.

Some are now so deficient in Vitamin D that they qualify as decorative indoor plants.

Then comes the fitness watch.

A tiny electronic device costing ₹30,000 whose sole purpose appears to be insulting its owner.

Poor sleep.

High stress.

Low recovery.

Inactivity detected.

At this point many professionals would prefer encouragement.

Instead the watch behaves like an elderly relative at a wedding.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Marriage in the Age of Microsoft Teams

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Indian marriage evolved around a simple assumption.

People would occasionally see each other.

The software industry decided to test that hypothesis.

Thus emerged the Two-IT-Income Couple.

On paper they represent modern success.

Two salaries.

Two careers.

Two cars.

Two laptops.

Two health insurance policies.

In practice they often resemble neighbouring startups sharing infrastructure.

Conversations become operational updates.

“Did you pay the electricity bill?”

“Client escalation.”

“Need groceries.”

“Production issue.”

“Let’s discuss later.”

Romance slowly adopts project-management language.

Date nights require calendar invitations.

Anniversaries require Outlook reminders.

Emotional conversations require stakeholder alignment.

One spouse works US hours.

The other works European hours.

Both occupy the same apartment while living in different time zones.

Traditional Indian parents remain bewildered.

Their daughter can manage a cloud infrastructure serving millions of users.

Yet somehow nobody has taught her the ancient art of producing perfectly circular chapatis.

Civilization, they conclude, is in decline.

While the couple’s economics improved, their chemistry for bonding declined and by the time they were ready for family, biology expired.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Childhood Outsourcing Industry

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The greatest irony emerges after parenthood.

The same economy that celebrates working mothers often makes motherhood operationally impossible.

Modern parenting increasingly resembles remote project management.

Children are monitored through CCTV.

Apps.

Notifications.

Location trackers.

School dashboards.

Parents observe childhood the way managers observe offshore teams.

Through metrics.

The daycare industry has become an unofficial extension of the software sector.

Children arrive early.

Leave late.

Grow up efficiently.

Parents compensate with expensive toys, subscriptions and guilt.

Large amounts of guilt.

Many children today know Marvel superheroes better than family history.

They can identify fictional universes across multiple continents.

Yet struggle to identify second cousins at family weddings.

Grandparents increasingly exist inside mobile-phone screens.

Family bonds survive.

But increasingly through scheduled video calls.

And through all this, women carry the heaviest burden.

Corporate culture expects uninterrupted productivity.

Society expects uninterrupted motherhood.

Relatives expect uninterrupted availability.

The laws of physics refuse cooperation.

Something always gives way.

Usually sleep.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Return-to-Office Comedy Festival

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Then came the pandemic.

For a brief glorious period, people imagined liberation.

Work from home.

No commuting.

More family time.

Greater flexibility.

The future had arrived.

Then reality appeared.

Work from home quickly became office from home.

The laptop migrated from desk to dining table.

Then bedroom.

Then vacation.

Then hospital waiting room.

Work entered every room of the house like an overenthusiastic relative who refuses to leave after Deepavali.

And just when everyone adapted, corporations announced:

Return to Office.

Employees who had successfully worked from home for three years were informed that collaboration now required physical presence.

This revelation coincidentally emerged around the same time companies realised they owned expensive office buildings.

An extraordinary coincidence.

Traffic returned.

Exhaustion returned.

Commuting returned.

The old normal returned.

Only older.

And more tired.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Real Estate Hunger Games

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Housing in India’s technology corridors deserves classification as performance art.

Advertisements show smiling families enjoying luxury lifestyles.

Reality involves spending two hours daily trapped behind a water tanker.

Apartments shrink.

Rents expand.

Infrastructure collapses.

Property owners develop the confidence of medieval kings.

Documentation requirements resemble intelligence-agency recruitment.

Single women endure particularly creative interrogations.

Who visits?

When do they visit?

Why do they visit?

Will they continue visiting?

One begins to suspect that renting an apartment requires greater scrutiny than obtaining a security clearance.

The irony remains delicious.

A woman trusted with sensitive global financial systems still requires approval from an apartment association secretary armed with a plastic chair and excessive authority.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The KPI of Happiness

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

And so we arrive at the central paradox.

The IT Revolution was a tremendous success.

It educated millions.

Created wealth.

Transformed women’s lives.

Expanded opportunity.

Modern India would be unimaginable without it.

But every balance sheet contains hidden entries.

The modern professional woman is more educated than her mother.

More independent than her grandmother.

More financially secure than entire generations before her.

Yet she often possesses less time.

Less community.

Less rest.

Less certainty.

The industry connected continents.

Sometimes it disconnected families.

It delivered salaries.

It consumed evenings.

It enabled home ownership.

It weakened neighbourhood life.

The old socialist India had many flaws.

It was slow.

Bureaucratic.

Overregulated.

Often frustrating.

But it understood something modern India occasionally forgets.

A society is not merely an economy.

A citizen is not merely a consumer.

And a human being is not merely a resource.

The planners who designed places like Neyveli planted libraries, parks, schools and rain trees because they believed prosperity meant more than income.

They believed people required culture.

Friendship.

Conversation.

Leisure.

Belonging.

Perhaps they were right.

Today, as neon lights continue glowing across India’s technology corridors long after midnight, one cannot help wondering whether we optimized ourselves for productivity while underinvesting in happiness.

The deliverables were completed.

The targets were met.

The dashboards turned green.

The appraisals were satisfactory.

The ESOPs vested.

The EMIs were paid.

And yet, somewhere deep inside the collective middle-class soul of India, a small voice still whispers:

*“All this is wonderful. But when exactly are we supposed to live?”*
